name: Lo-Toga
confidence_why: Lo-Toga has no published grammar or phonology, and of the six François items read (2005, 2007, the 2020 dictionary, the Pangloss corpus, Krauße & François 2023 and 2024) only the historical article François 2005 touches stress, with an areal remark that northern Vanuatu words are now stressed on the final syllable and that Lo-Toga centralizes any vowel outside primary stress, so no synchronic Lo-Toga rule can be stated and any placement would be an inference rather than a description.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim in the François 2005 text we hold layer at the stated sections. (2) The record rests on a 2005 historical-comparative article, but that is the best there is: Glottolog, HAL and François's own publication list show no grammar, grammar sketch (beyond Codrington 1885, which I re-read and which has no accent statement) or phonology of Lo-Toga; the explicit last-non-schwa-vowel rule is published for the sister language Hiw only. Three further François items downloaded now (2007 noun articles; Krauße & François 2023, 2024) are silent on Lo-Toga word-stress placement, as is the online dictionary. (3) The not determinable coding is therefore correct and cannot be improved from published sources; the only refinement worth adding to the prose rule is François 2005 sec. 5.1.1 ('Hiu and Lo-Toga.. tend to centralize any vowel that does not receive primary stress') alongside the a

sources.quote: Same diachronic penultimate-stress statements as the 2023 paper; nothing synchronic for Lo-Toga.

sources.citation: Krauße, Daniel & Alexandre François (2023). The road to opacity: Reflexes of Proto-Oceanic *-akin in northern Vanuatu. NUSA 74: 35-80.
sources.quote: Only diachronic: PTB *-áɣi / *'CVCV 'with penultimate stress' reduced to CVC; *-áCi > LTG /-ɛC/. No synchronic Lo-Toga stress rule.

sources.quote: Entries give phonetic forms (e.g. ake [akə]) without stress marks; no phonology/orthography introduction is online (240 entries, 'in progress').

sources.quote: 'the article lacks its own primary stress, being prosodically integrated to the following noun: e.g., LTG n=huw rat' -- proclitic status only; nothing on where word stress falls in Lo-Toga.

sources.note: No published synchronic stress statement exists for Lo-Toga; the only route past not determinable is an in-house acoustic check of whether stress falls on the last full (non-schwa) vowel as in Hiw (François 2010) -- the open Pangloss audio is the material for that. Not a citable description, so low priority.

sources.citation: François, Alexandre. 2011. Social ecology and language history in the northern Vanuatu linkage: A tale of divergence and convergence. Journal of Historical Linguistics 1(2): 175-246.
sources.note: No lexical or grammatical tone is mentioned for any of the 17 languages; sec. 4.2.1 (phonological diversity: inventories, phonotactics) ends with the only pitch statement, an intonational one: the two Torres languages (Hiw, Lo-Toga) and the Gaua languages mark polar questions with a falling contour where the others use rising pitch (p. 195); stress appears only diachronically (metaphony correlated with stress, p. 194).

tone.quote: Even intonation can differ across languages. Whereas most languages express polar questions with a rising pitch, two sets of languages (the two Torres languages, plus those of Gaua) provide these questions with a falling contour.
tone.locator: p. 195, sec. 4.2.1, end of the phonology overview

sources.citation: François, Alexandre. 2010. Pragmatic demotion and clause dependency: On two atypical subordinating strategies in Lo-Toga and Hiw (Torres, Vanuatu). In Isabelle Bril (ed.), Clause Linking and Clause Hierarchy: Syntax and Pragmatics (Studies in Language Companion Series 121), 499-548. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
sources.note: A morphosyntax chapter with no phonology section beyond spelling conventions (fn., p. 2) and no mention of lexical or grammatical tone; pitch enters only as sentence prosody: Subjunctive main clauses are licensed by the order/exclamation intonation ('a high pitch plateau ending in an instant fall', p. 20), and Background-Perfect clefts show a contrastive accent on the last stressed syllable followed by a fall in pitch and intensity (p. 42, Lo-Toga ex. 89 with phonetic transcription).

tone.quote: On the other hand, the prosody of (35a–b), which is characteristic of orders and exclamatory sentences – a high pitch plateau ending in an instant fall – makes the sentence grammatical. In my interpretation, the particular suprasegmental profile of the sentence is the locus where the needed illocutionary force is lodged, and must be sought.
